title: Declaration merging and module augmentation
description: Learn how declaration merging and module augmentation let you extend third-party types safely in React and TypeScript projects.

data.text: Sometimes you need to add properties to a type you do not control. Maybe a library forgot to export a type you need, or you want to add custom fields to a framework object. TypeScript lets you do this safely with declaration merging and module augmentation.

When two interfaces share the same name in the same scope, TypeScript merges their properties automatically. This is the simplest form of declaration merging and it works across files in the same project.

data.title: Merging Interfaces
data.content: Extending an interface in another file

data.text: Module augmentation lets you add to a module exported by another package. This is how you extend NextAuth types, add custom fields to React context values, or enhance library interfaces without forking the source.

data.title: Augmenting a Module
data.content: Adding fields to an external module

data.text: Module augmentation appears frequently in React applications. You may use it to add custom properties to context values, extend CSS module types, or provide types for untyped JavaScript libraries.

items: Extend NextAuth session and user types
Add custom fields to library modules
Add properties to React context values

data.title: Extending CSS Module Types
Use Global Augmentation Sparingly
data.text: Module augmentation is powerful but can create hidden dependencies. Keep augmentation files in one place, document why each extension exists, and prefer composition when possible.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Interfaces with the same name are merged automatically
Module augmentation extends third-party types safely
Use it for NextAuth, CSS modules, and context values
Keep augmentation files organized and documented
data.takeaway: Declaration merging lets you make unchangeable types fit your application without losing type safety.
